The Islamic calendar, also called the Hijri calendar, is a purely lunar calendar used throughout the Islamic world to date events and determine religious observances. Unlike the solar Gregorian calendar, its months drift relative to the seasons, anchored instead to the Hijra—Prophet Muhammad's migration from Mecca to Medina in 622 CE.

The calendar is purely lunar, with each month being either twenty-nine or thirty days, matching actual lunar phases, making the year approximately 354 days—about eleven days shorter than the solar year. Year 1 AH, Anno Hegirae, corresponds to 622 CE, the date of the Hijra. Dates are often written as 1445 AH to distinguish them from the Common Era. Because the year is shorter than the solar year, Islamic months rotate through all seasons over a thirty-three-year cycle, so Ramadan is not always in the same season.

Ramadan, the ninth month, is the Islamic holy month of fasting and spiritual renewal, and the exact dates shift backward ten to eleven days each solar year. The Hijri New Year falls on the first day of Muharram, the first lunar month, a date that changes relative to the Gregorian calendar annually. The calendar coexists globally with the Gregorian calendar, and Islamic-majority countries often use both systems for legal, administrative, and religious purposes. Month names carry religious and historical significance—Rajab is the month of pilgrimage, and Dhu al-Hijjah is when the Hajj pilgrimage to Mecca occurs.

The lunar year's shorter length means Muslims celebrate Islamic holidays at different times each solar year, with ancient Ramadans in summer and later Ramadans in winter—a feature central to Islamic practice. Modern Islamic institutions use astronomical calculations to determine month boundaries precisely, though some communities still rely on actual moon sighting, called ruyat al-hilal, for traditional observance.
